title: Metal Gear Acid
subtitle: Snake learns to plan a hand of cards
summary: Metal Gear Acid is Konami's PSP tactical stealth game, first released in Japan on 16 December 2004. It places Snake in an alternate story outside the main Metal Gear continuity, replacing continuous action with turns governed by a deck of cards. Movement, weapons and special actions depend on the hand available at that moment. The player recognises familiar equipment and characters, but uses them as parts of a plan. Its arrival on a handheld becomes an opportunity to reconsider how a stealth mission can be organised rather than simply reproduce the console games on a smaller screen.
body: Metal Gear Acid is Konami's PSP tactical stealth game, first released in Japan on 16 December 2004. It places Snake in an alternate story outside the main Metal Gear continuity, replacing continuous action with turns governed by a deck of cards. Movement, weapons and special actions depend on the hand available at that moment. The player recognises familiar equipment and characters, but uses them as parts of a plan. Its arrival on a handheld becomes an opportunity to reconsider how a stealth mission can be organised rather than simply reproduce the console games on a smaller screen.

Before a mission, the player prepares decks for the characters. During a turn, a card can be used for its particular effect or spent to move across the map. That choice gives an apparently valuable attack another possible purpose: it might be more important to reach cover now than preserve a weapon for later. A hand contains only a limited selection, so the intended plan must adapt to what has been drawn. The player balances the route through the area with the resources needed when an enemy finally has to be confronted.

Shinta Nojiri directed and designed the project, with Nobuko Toda, Shuichi Kobori and Akihiro Honda composing the music. Cards draw on the wider Metal Gear series, making the deck a collection of recognisable references as well as a set of tactical tools. The game supplies its cards through normal play rather than requiring separate purchases. North American and European PSP releases followed in 2005, and a sequel arrived later that year in Japan. Acid's distinctive idea is to make preparation visible in the hand, where every possible action also competes with the need to move.
